catalog_quote: 3.1.2 Word-internal metrical structure. Since syncope and accentual processes are rare in Kelenga, there is not much to say about foot structure. CvCvCv words do not syncopate systematically to CvCCv, although when C2 is r it allows optional syncope of the second vowel: màrìfá-à ~ màrfá-à 'rifle'. There is no well-defined stress system as such. Whereas some languages of the zone allow only one H-toned peak (whether on a single mora or syllable or spread over multiple syllables), Kelenga allows two peaks in noun stems, as in téèndáŋ-ɔ̀ 'hamerkop (bird)' and tómóndìgí-ì 'ricin (shrub)'. There is no sensitivity to overall prosodic weight of stems in affixal morphology. ... [p. 45] Since prefixes do not occur in Kelenga morphology and since there is no well-defined stress system, it is not possible to distinguish proclitics from prefixes by phonological criteria. ... new_statements.quote: 3. Die tonale Differenzierung Nomen-Verb im Kelinga-Bozo. Auch im Kelinga-Bozo unterscheiden sich Lexeme mit verbaler oder nominaler Funktion rein tonal. Im Gegensatz zu den bisher besprochenen Sprachen erfolgt dies jedoch nicht durch die Suffigierung eines rein tonalen [...] sondern durch die Invertierung des gesamten Worttons: jeder Tiefton wird zu einem Hochton, jeder Hochton zu einem Tiefton, aufsteigende Töne werden zu fallenden und fallende zu aufsteigenden. [p. 24:] Doch nicht nur die Wortklasse determiniert die tonale Realisation des Wortstamms, sondern auch die Zugehörigkeit zu Subjekt oder Prädikat.
new_statements.translation: 3. The tonal differentiation noun-verb in Kelinga-Bozo. In Kelinga-Bozo too, lexemes with verbal or nominal function differ purely tonally. In contrast to the languages discussed so far, however, this is not achieved by suffixing a purely tonal [...] but by inverting the entire word tone: every low tone becomes a high tone, every high tone a low tone, rising tones become falling and falling tones rising. [p. 24:] Yet not only word class determines the tonal realisation of the word stem, but also membership in the subject or the predicate.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kelenga has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements, so nothing to agree with or contradict. Ebermann supplies the type: a lexical- and grammatical-tone language (H, L, rising, falling) with wholesale tone inversion by word class and by subject/predicate position, and is silent on stress proper. Same variety as the catalog entry: Ebermann's 'Kelinga (auch Hainyaxo genannt)' = Glottolog Hainyaxo Bozo [bzx] = Heath's Kelenga.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kelinga (Hainyaxo) Bozo is treated throughout as a tone language: words carry high, low and rising/falling contour tones, and the whole word-tone melody is inverted as a grammatical device (verbal vs nominal function of a lexeme; predicative vs non-predicative position of a nominal, p. 25). The article says nothing about word stress or accent; the terms Akzent, Betonung, Wortakzent, Druck, Intensität, Prominenz, Stress and accent return no hit anywhere in the indexed 234-page volume.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (no stress discussed at all).
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal, not stress-related: the tone of xele/kele is wholly conditioned by its tonal environment (p. 24, fn. 12); for many and especially older Kelinga speakers the grammatical function of tone goes beyond marking word category (p. 24); adjectives used purely nominally take the inverted tone (p. 24: loxo 'young, small' vs a loxo 'he is small, young'); Kelinga speakers who also speak Bambara pronounce nominal-function lexemes exactly as Bambara speakers do but verbal-function lexemes with inverted tone (p. 26).
new_statements.identity_note: Ebermann p. 15: "Das Kelinga (auch Hainyaxo genannt) ist eine dialektale Variante des Bozo und gehört damit zu den Mandesprachen und innerhalb der Mandesprachen zur Nord-West-Untergruppe". His data come from his own fieldwork in Mali (his CV lists Jan-Mar 2003 fieldwork among Bambara, Bozo and Fulbe in the Macina region, project SIKWA). Glottolog maps 'Kelinga = Hainyaxo' to Hainyaxo Bozo [bzx] = hain1253, i.e. the same variety Heath 2023 calls Kelenga; the work compares it with Bambara/Mandenkan, Northern Samo, Bobo, Jo and Boko-Busa, but the quoted section is about Kelinga itself.

audit.reasoning: The no-word-stress coding rests on the only reference grammar of the language (Heath 2023, 619 pp, open access), which we hold; the deciding sentences ('There is no well-defined stress system as such', 'the absence of stress') are verbatim at sec. 3.1.2 p. 21 and sec. 3.5 p. 45-46, and sec. 3.6 confirms prosody is lexical H/L tone with stem melodies. Heath's scattered remarks attributing low pitch of particles bí/gà to 'lack of stress' (pp. ~296, 459) are phrase-level allegro effects on grammatical particles, not a word-stress system, and do not disturb the classification. Glottolog and Zenodo show no newer or more specialised prosodic study. Minor locator nit only: the clitics sentence sits at the p. 45/46 boundary. no reclassification, no upgrade needed.
